name: הפרדת משתנים – פתרון כללי עם tanh (ב) (באנגלית)
questiontext:
Solve the following differential equation: \[ \frac{dy}{dx} - {{CT:0}} -{{CT:1}}x^2+{{CT:2}}y^2+y^2x^2 = 0. \] Use the letter \(c\) to denote the arbitrary constant occuring in the general solution.
y(x) = [[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]]
generalfeedback:
Rearranging the differential equation gives \[\frac{dy}{dx}-{{CT:1}}({{CT:2}}+x^2)+y^2({{CT:2}}+x^2)=0\] and therefore \[\frac{dy}{dx}=({{CT:1}}-y^2)({{CT:2}}+x^2),\] so that 
\[\frac{dy}{{{CT:1}}-y^2}=({{CT:2}}+x^2)dx.\]
Integrating both sides yields: \[\int\frac{dy}{{{CT:1}}-y^2}=\int({{CT:2}}+x^2)dx\]
To integrate the left hand side, rearrange \[\frac{dy}{{{CT:1}}-y^2}=\frac{dy}{{{CT:1}}(1-\frac{y^2}{{CT:1}})}\] Let \(\frac{y}{{CT:3}} = \tanh(u)\) \[\frac{dy}{{CT:3}}=(1-\tanh^2(u))du = (1-\frac{y^2}{{CT:1}})du\] \[\frac{dy}{(1-\frac{y^2}{{CT:1}})}={{CT:3}}du.\]
Therefore \[\int\frac{dy}{{{CT:1}}-y^2}=\frac{1}{{CT:1}}\int\frac{dy}{{CT:4}}=\frac{1}{{CT:1}}\int{{CT:3}}du=\frac{u}{{CT:3}}.\]
Integrating the right hand side gives \[\int({{CT:2}}+x^2)dx={{CT:2}}x+\frac{x^3}{3}+c.\] Therefore \[\frac{u}{{CT:3}}={{CT:2}}x+\frac{x^3}{3}+c,\] so that \[u={{CT:3}}\left({{CT:2}}x+\frac{x^3}{3}+c\right)\] and hence \[\tanh(u)=\tanh\left({{CT:3}}\left({{CT:2}}x+\frac{x^3}{3}+c\right)\right)\]
Therefore \[\frac{y}{{CT:3}}=\tanh\left({{CT:3}}\left({{CT:2}}x+\frac{x^3}{3}+c\right)\right)\] and \[y={{CT:5}}\]

on_false.feedback: Your answer does not satisfy the differential equation.

on_true.feedback: Your answer does satisfy the differential equation, and does contain a constant. However it is in a strange form. Perhaps you could ask your tutor about how to write this in an equivalent form which is "simpler".

on_false.feedback: Your answer does satisfy the differential equation but either does not have a constant specified or you did not use \(c\) (small case) as instructed.
